text: London noon solar elevation at the June solstice is about 62 degrees (90 minus latitude 51.5 plus obliquity 23.44)
as_written: about sixty-two degrees above the horizon
source: Computed from London's latitude and Earth's obliquity (NASA Earth Fact Sheet); standard solar-geometry formula as in the Astronomical Almanac

text: London daylight at the June solstice lasts about 16.5 hours
as_written: about sixteen and a half hours
source: HM Nautical Almanac Office / Royal Observatory Greenwich sunrise and sunset tables for London

text: London noon solar elevation at the December solstice is about 15 degrees (90 minus 51.5 minus 23.44)
as_written: about fifteen degrees above the rooftops
source: Computed from London's latitude and Earth's obliquity (NASA Earth Fact Sheet)

text: Earth's axial tilt is about 23.4 degrees
as_written: about twenty-three and a half degrees
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (obliquity 23.44 degrees)

text: Moving the tilt to the opposite side requires turning the axis by twice the tilt, about 47 degrees
as_written: about forty-seven degrees
source: Derived: 2 x 23.44 degrees, using the NASA Earth Fact Sheet obliquity

text: Earth's rotational kinetic energy is about 2 x 10^29 joules
as_written: two times ten to the twenty-ninth joules
source: Computed from Earth's moment of inertia (about 8.04 x 10^37 kg m^2) and angular velocity (7.292 x 10^-5 rad/s); values from the IERS Conventions and NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: Sunlight intercepted by Earth is about 174 petawatts
as_written: one hundred seventy-four petawatts
source: NASA Earth Energy Budget; solar constant of about 1361 W/m^2 times Earth's cross-section (Kopp and Lean 2011, SORCE/TIM)

text: Earth's rotational energy equals roughly 39,000 years of total incident sunlight
as_written: nearly forty thousand years of every ray of sunlight
source: Derived: 2.1 x 10^29 J divided by 1.74 x 10^17 W, using the IERS and NASA values above

text: At the equator on the June solstice the noon Sun is about 66.5 degrees above the horizon (90 minus 23.44)
as_written: about sixty-six and a half degrees up
source: Computed from obliquity, NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: The Arctic Circle lies at about 66.5 degrees north
as_written: about sixty-six and a half degrees north
source: IERS / Astronomical Almanac; complement of the obliquity, 90 minus 23.44

text: Sine of 62 degrees is about 0.88; sine of 15 degrees is about 0.26
as_written: about point eight eight
source: Trigonometry; standard Lambert cosine law for insolation on a horizontal surface

text: Sine of 15 degrees is about 0.26, so ground receives less than a third as much energy per square meter
as_written: less than a third of what it did a minute ago
source: Trigonometry; Lambert cosine law (0.26/0.88 is about 0.29)

text: London winter-solstice daylight is just under 8 hours, so night exceeds 16 hours
as_written: just under eight
source: HM Nautical Almanac Office / Royal Observatory Greenwich sunrise and sunset tables for London

text: The top ~3 meters of ocean hold as much heat as the whole atmosphere
as_written: top three meters of the ocean hold as much heat as the entire atmosphere
source: NOAA National Ocean Service / NOAA Climate.gov, ocean heat capacity

text: Land temperatures typically peak about a month after the solstice
as_written: about a month after the solstice
source: NOAA/NWS climatology on seasonal temperature lag

text: Fresh snow reflects roughly 80 to 90 percent of incoming sunlight
as_written: eighty to ninety percent of the sunlight
source: NSIDC, All About Sea Ice: albedo of snow and ice

text: Antarctica holds about 90 percent of Earth's ice
as_written: about ninety percent of all the ice on Earth
source: NSIDC, Quick Facts on Ice Sheets

text: Earth's perihelion distance is about 147 million km
as_written: about one hundred forty-seven million kilometers
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (147.09 million km)

text: Earth's aphelion distance is about 152 million km
as_written: about one hundred fifty-two million kilometers
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (152.10 million km)

text: Perihelion is in early January and aphelion in early July
as_written: In early January, Earth is at its closest
source: U.S. Naval Observatory, Earth's Seasons and Apsides table

text: The aphelion-perihelion difference is about 5 million km
as_written: five million kilometer difference
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (152.10 minus 147.09 million km)

text: Earth receives about 7 percent more sunlight at perihelion than aphelion
as_written: about seven percent more sunshine in January than in July
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet; inverse-square derivation (152.10/147.09 squared is about 1.069)

text: The June solstice is a couple of weeks before aphelion
as_written: a couple of weeks before Earth reaches its farthest point
source: U.S. Naval Observatory, Earth's Seasons and Apsides table

text: About 40 percent of the Northern Hemisphere is land
as_written: About forty percent of the northern hemisphere is land
source: NOAA / CIA World Factbook land-ocean hemisphere statistics (about 39 percent)

text: About 19 percent of the Southern Hemisphere is land
as_written: about nineteen percent
source: NOAA / CIA World Factbook land-ocean hemisphere statistics (about 19 percent)

text: The Southern Hemisphere is over 80 percent ocean
as_written: over eighty percent ocean
source: Derived from the 19 percent land figure above

text: Global mean surface temperature is nearly 4 C warmer in July than January
as_written: nearly four degrees Celsius over January
source: Berkeley Earth monthly absolute-temperature climatology (about 12.0 C in January versus about 15.9 C in July)

text: Annual mean insolation depends on eccentricity and not on precession
as_written: hardly changes, because that total depends on the shape of the orbit
source: Berger 1978, Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences; Milankovitch insolation theory

text: Verkhoyansk's record low is about minus 68 C
as_written: about minus sixty-eight degrees Celsius
source: WMO Archive of Weather and Climate Extremes (minus 67.8 C, February 1892)

text: Verkhoyansk reached 38 C in June 2020
as_written: in June of twenty twenty it reached thirty-eight
source: WMO Archive of Weather and Climate Extremes (38.0 C, 20 June 2020)

text: The Verkhoyansk record range exceeds 100 degrees
as_written: a swing of more than a hundred degrees
source: Derived from the WMO extremes (38.0 minus minus 67.8 is about 106 C)

text: Milankovitch theory emphasises northern summer insolation for ice ages
as_written: points at northern summer sunshine and not winter cold
source: Milankovitch 1941; Hays, Imbrie and Shackleton 1976, Science

text: Greenland ice holds about 7 meters of sea-level equivalent
as_written: about seven meters
source: NASA / IMBIE; Morlighem et al. 2017, Geophysical Research Letters (7.4 m)

text: Arctic terns migrate about 70,000 km per year
as_written: about seventy thousand kilometers
source: Egevang et al. 2010, PNAS, tracking Arctic tern migration (mean about 70,900 km)

text: Climatic precession cycle lasts roughly 21,000 years
as_written: roughly twenty-one thousand years
source: Berger and Loutre 1991; NASA Earth Observatory, Milankovitch Cycles

text: The tropical year is about 365.2422 days
as_written: three hundred sixty-five point two four two two days
source: IERS Conventions / Astronomical Almanac

text: The anomalistic year is about 365.2596 days
as_written: three hundred sixty-five point two five nine six days
source: Astronomical Almanac, Explanatory Supplement

text: The anomalistic year exceeds the tropical year by about 25 minutes
as_written: The gap is about twenty-five minutes
source: Derived: 0.0174 days is about 25 minutes, from the two values above

text: Perihelion fell in northern summer about 10 to 11 thousand years ago
as_written: about ten or eleven thousand years back
source: Berger and Loutre 1991, Quaternary Science Reviews insolation solution; half of the roughly 21,000-year precession cycle

text: African Humid Period lasted from about 14,800 to about 5,500 years ago
as_written: from nearly fifteen thousand years ago until about five and a half thousand years ago
source: deMenocal et al. 2000, Quaternary Science Reviews

text: Dust record off Mauritania shows an abrupt end of the African Humid Period within centuries
as_written: within a few centuries
source: deMenocal et al. 2000, Quaternary Science Reviews

text: Other records indicate regionally gradual or patchy drying
as_written: a patchwork, with some regions drying gradually
source: Kröpelin et al. 2008, Science (Lake Yoa, gradual); Shanahan et al. 2015, Nature Geoscience

text: About 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust deposit on the Amazon yearly
as_written: about twenty-eight million tons
source: Yu et al. 2015, Geophysical Research Letters (NASA CALIPSO satellite data)

text: That dust carries about 22,000 tons of phosphorus, comparable to Amazon losses
as_written: about twenty-two thousand tons of phosphorus
source: Yu et al. 2015, Geophysical Research Letters (NASA CALIPSO satellite data)

text: Ice-age cycles shifted to roughly 100,000-year periodicity over the last million years or so
as_written: roughly one hundred thousand years
source: Lisiecki and Raymo 2005, Paleoceanography (LR04 benchmark); Mid-Pleistocene Transition literature

text: Obliquity cycle lasts about 41,000 years
as_written: roughly forty-one thousand years
source: NASA Earth Observatory, Milankovitch Cycles

text: Earth's tilt varies between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees
as_written: between about twenty-two point one and twenty-four point five degrees
source: NASA Earth Observatory, Milankovitch Cycles

text: Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees
as_written: tipped about ninety-eight degrees
source: NASA Uranus Fact Sheet (97.77 degrees)

text: Uranus's tilt is probably from a giant collision, though debated
as_written: probably by a giant collision long ago, though even that is still debated
source: Kegerreis et al. 2018, The Astrophysical Journal; Rogoszinski and Hamilton 2020

text: Perihelion will fall in northern summer again in about ten thousand years
as_written: in about ten thousand years
source: Berger and Loutre 1991 insolation solution; half of the roughly 21,000-year cycle
